0.title: The Letter of Joy: Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
0.overview:
Philippians is the most personal and warmest of Paul’s letters — a love letter to the church that had been his closest partner in the gospel from the very beginning of the European mission. He wrote it from prison, most likely in Rome, facing the real possibility of execution. And yet the letter’s dominant note is joy. “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice” (4:4). The word “joy” or “rejoice” appears sixteen times in four chapters. This is not the forced cheerfulness of a man in denial; it is the deep, settled gladness of a man who has found that Christ is sufficient for every circumstance, including chains, including death.

Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia — the first European city Paul evangelized (Acts 16), where the gospel arrived through a riverside prayer meeting, a wealthy cloth merchant named Lydia, a slave girl freed from a spirit of divination, and a jailer shaken to conversion by an earthquake. The church that emerged from these unlikely beginnings remained Paul’s most generous supporter: “no church entered into partnership with me in giving and receiving except you only” (4:15). When Paul was imprisoned, they sent Epaphroditus with a gift — and now Paul sends this letter back with him, full of gratitude, theology, and pastoral instruction.

Where was Paul imprisoned when he wrote? Three places have been suggested. Some argue for Ephesus, because it was near enough to Philippi for the several journeys the letter implies; others for Caesarea, where Paul was held for two years (Acts 24:27). The more likely answer is Rome, around AD 60–62. Paul mentions the whole imperial guard (1:13) and those of Caesar’s household (4:22), and he faces a verdict that could end in death with no further appeal, which fits Rome, where he had already appealed to Caesar, better than either alternative.

The letter’s theological heart is the great Christ hymn of chapter 2 (vv. 6–11), which may be the earliest christological poem in the New Testament — pre-Pauline in origin, perhaps already sung in the churches before Paul wrote. It traces the arc of the Son of God from the heights of divine equality, through the descent of incarnation and the depths of a slave’s death on a cross, to the exaltation at which every knee bows and every tongue confesses. This is not merely doxology; it is the pattern of Christian existence. The community that sings this hymn is called to embody it: the same self-emptying, other-serving, glory-surrendering mind that was in Christ Jesus is to be in them.

The letter’s other great passage is the biographical testimony of chapter 3 (vv. 4–11), where Paul lists his impressive Jewish credentials — circumcised on the eighth day, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Pharisee, blameless under the law — and then counts them all as loss, as rubbish, as dung (skybala) compared to “the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord.” This is the gospel of grace arriving at personal address: not the abstract doctrine of justification but the lived reality of a man for whom Christ has become everything, and everything else has become nothing by comparison.

Philippians is the answer to the question: what does a life shaped by the gospel actually look like? It looks like partnership rather than rivalry, like humility rather than self-promotion, like contentment rather than anxiety, like pressing forward rather than dwelling on the past, like the peace of God that passes understanding rather than the turmoil of the person whose security rests on circumstances. It is the most beautiful portrait of mature Christian life in Paul’s letters — and it was painted by a man in chains, who could see the executioner’s sword, and who wrote: “to live is Christ, and to die is gain.”

1.title: To Live Is Christ: Partnership, Prison, and the Advance of the Gospel
1.overview:
Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, settled by retired soldiers, and the first church Paul planted in Europe (Acts 16): a businesswoman named Lydia, a converted jailer, and a few others. About ten years later Paul writes from prison, probably in Rome, to thank them for a gift and to steady them under opposition. It is the warmest of his letters, full of joy.

Chapter 1 thanks God for their partnership in the gospel and states a great certainty: God, who began a good work in them, will finish it. Paul prays that their love will grow in knowledge and discernment. Then he reports from his cell: his chains have advanced the gospel through the imperial guard, other believers have grown bolder, and even rivals who preach to spite him are preaching Christ, so he rejoices. Facing a possible death sentence, he writes, “to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain,” yet expects to stay for their sake. He ends by calling them to live as citizens worthy of the gospel, standing together, unafraid, knowing that suffering for Christ is itself a gift of grace.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, greet all God’s people at Philippi, with the overseers and deacons: grace and peace. Paul thanks God every time he remembers them, praying with joy because of their partnership in the gospel from the first day. He is confident that God, who began a good work in them, will complete it on the day of Christ. It is right for him to feel this way, since they share in God’s grace with him in his imprisonment and his defence of the gospel. God knows how he longs for them with Christ’s affection. He prays that their love will grow more and more in knowledge and insight, so that they can discern what is best and be pure and blameless for the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus, to God’s glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
The God Who Finishes What He Starts

Philippians 1:6 is among the strongest statements of perseverance in the New Testament, and its whole force lies in the subject of the two verbs. God began the good work; God will complete it. The believer is the field, not the farmer. Reformed theology has always insisted that perseverance is not the Christian’s achievement but God’s gift — the same grace that opens a heart keeps it, and the same power that raised Christ is at work in everyone united to him.

This is not a doctrine that makes effort pointless; it is what makes effort reasonable. Paul will command the Philippians to work out their own salvation with fear and trembling, and in the same breath tell them that it is God who works in them both to will and to work (2:12–13). The two sentences are not in tension. A Christian labours precisely because the outcome is guaranteed by someone else, which is the only ground on which anyone has ever laboured with hope. Assurance rests not on the strength of our grip but on the certainty of his (John 10:28–29).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Philippians had every reason for anxiety. Their apostle was in chains, their city was a Roman garrison town where the imperial cult was a civic expectation, opposition was real (v.28), and the congregation had a quarrel in it that Paul will have to name by the end of the letter (4:2). His answer is not to reassure them about their circumstances or to praise their track record, but to point them to the character of the God who started the work.

Now: The Christian who lies awake wondering whether his faith will last is asking a question about the wrong grip. If perseverance depends on the tenacity of the believer, the honest answer is bleak; every one of us has already discovered how quickly we let go. Verse 6 puts the question the other way round — will God let go? — and answers it with “I am sure of this.” And verse 9 supplies the prayer to pray for the people you love: not that their week would be easy, but that their love would grow eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, To all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the overseers and deacons: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, to all God’s holy people in Christ Jesus at Philippi, together with the overseers and deacons: grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

The church at the river. Paul found no synagogue in Philippi, so on the Sabbath he went down to the river where women met to pray. The church began with Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth, and the jailer who put Paul in the stocks and then washed his wounds (Acts 16:13–34). A businesswoman and a jailer.

Slaves. Douloi, not “apostle”. The word Paul will use of Christ, who took “the form of a servant” (2:7). Before asking them to have Christ’s mind, he shows them a man who has begun to.

Saints. Hagioi: not a rank for exceptional godliness, but where they are, in Christ. The jailer as much as Lydia. And “all”: Paul says “all” again and again in a letter that will have to name two women who cannot get along (4:2).

Overseers and deacons. No other letter greets officers. Plural overseers: in the New Testament “overseer” and “elder” name one office (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7), held by a group. Named after the saints: among them, not over them.

Grace and peace. Favour first, then the end of the war it creates (Romans 5:1). Much religion tries to manufacture peace while leaving grace unsettled.
verseByVerse.note: Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, the first church Paul founded in Europe. He wrote from prison, probably in Rome. “Overseers” (elders) and deacons were the two offices of leadership.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank my God in all my remembrance of you, always in every prayer of mine for you all making my prayer with joy, because of your partnership in the gospel from the first day until now.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I thank my God every time I remember you. In all my prayers for all of you, I always pray with joy, because of your partnership in the gospel from the first day until now.

Every memory. Paul was beaten and jailed in this city and knew its quarrels, yet no memory of Philippi has to be stepped around.

Partnership. Koinōnia: going in together on a venture; in ordinary Greek, a business partnership. They had put money and themselves into the gospel (4:15–16). Shareholders, not an audience.

What it cost. The Macedonian churches gave out of “extreme poverty … beyond their means”, begging to take part (2 Corinthians 8:1–5). Paul thanks God not for their capacity but for what they did with little.

From the first day. A riverbank, an earthquake, a jail, a magistrate’s apology, years of gifts carried along the Via Egnatia. History between Christians matters.

Thanks before requests, and with joy. Is praying for someone a gladness to you, or an item on a list?

On a Tuesday. Thank God by name for the people who have partnered with you in the gospel over the years. Then tell one of them.
verseByVerse.note: The Philippians had supported Paul financially from the start.

verseByVerse.quote: And I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am confident of this, that he who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus.

God’s work. Two verbs, “began” and “will complete”, with one subject. He opened the account; he will close it. Not a builder who runs out of money at the second storey.

A good work. All of it: the light coming on, the verdict “not guilty”, and the slow remaking going on now, usually more visible to others than to you.

The day of Jesus Christ. Not the day you die, or the day you finally beat your sin. The day he appears.

The wrong question. “Will I still be a Christian in twenty years?” asks about your grip. Honestly answered, probably not. This verse answers a different question: will God let go? Answer: “I am sure.”

Can a believer be lost? Arminian Christians hold that a believer can turn away and perish, pointing to Hebrews 6:4–6 and to “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (2:12). The warnings are real. But the next verse gives the reason the working out succeeds: “it is God who works in you” (2:13). What God begins, he finishes. Those who fall away for good show the work never began (1 John 2:19).

On a Tuesday. A drowning man held by a lifeguard is safe not because of how well he grips but because he is gripped (John 10:28). That does not make effort pointless; it makes it hopeful.

verseByVerse.quote: It is right for me to feel this way about you all, because I hold you in my heart, for you are all partakers with me of grace, both in my imprisonment and in the defense and confirmation of the gospel. For God is my witness, how I yearn for you all with the affection of Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is right for me to feel this way about all of you, since I have you in my heart. Whether I am in chains or defending and confirming the gospel, all of you share in God’s grace with me. God can testify how I long for all of you with the affection of Christ Jesus.

Partakers. The root of koinōnia. They sent money and a man (2:25), so the ministry in Rome is theirs. The soldier chained to Paul heard the gospel partly because a church in Macedonia paid for Paul to be there.

Defence and confirmation. Courtroom words: apologia, the speech for the defence; bebaiōsis, legal establishing. Paul is on trial, and a church eight hundred miles away stands in the dock with him. Those who pray for and fund a work they never see are not on the sidelines.

Affection. Splanchna, the inward organs: the ache in the gut when you think of someone you love and cannot reach.

Of Christ. Not merely strong feeling, but Christ’s own love for them running through Paul. No one can verify an inward ache, so he calls God to witness.

On a Tuesday. When you think of the people in your church, does anything in you move? Ask Christ to share his affection for them with you.

verseByVerse.quote: And it is my prayer that your love may abound more and more, with knowledge and all discernment, so that you may approve what is excellent, and so be pure and blameless for the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is my prayer: that your love may abound more and more in knowledge and depth of insight, so that you may be able to discern what is best and may be pure and blameless for the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.

Not easier circumstances. Paul prays that their love will grow, and qualifies how.

Love with banks. A flooding verb: overflowing. But a river without banks is a disaster. The banks: epignōsis, settled knowledge, and aisthēsis, trained perception. Love that is warm and can see.

Two failures. Love without discernment cannot say no, is taken in by every plausible teacher, and calls its softness kindness. Discernment without love spots error at fifty paces and has a shrinking heart. Sentimentality, and something close to cruelty.

What is excellent. Dokimazein, to test and approve, like assaying metal; “the things that differ”. Most hard choices are not between good and evil but between good and best.

Pure. Eilikrinēs, perhaps from judging by sunlight: what it appears when the light gets behind it.

Through Jesus Christ. Fruit not manufactured, but coming through him as sap through a branch (John 15:4–5).

A textual note. One early papyrus reads “to the glory of God and praise of me”, apparently a slip. All others read “to the glory and praise of God”.

On a Tuesday. Pray this for someone instead of praying their week goes smoothly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–26 — The Chains, the Rivals, and the Choice
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What has happened to Paul has actually advanced the gospel: the whole palace guard knows he is in chains for Christ, and most believers have become bolder in speaking God’s word. Some preach Christ out of envy and rivalry, hoping to add to his trouble; others out of love, knowing he is there to defend the gospel. Either way Christ is preached, and Paul rejoices. Through their prayers and the Spirit’s help, this will turn out for his deliverance. He hopes not to be ashamed, but that Christ will be honoured in his body, by life or by death. For to him, to live is Christ and to die is gain. He is torn: he longs to depart and be with Christ, which is far better, but staying is more necessary for them. So he expects to remain, for their progress and joy in the faith.
verseByVerse.theology:
Providence: The Chains Were Not a Setback

What Paul reports here is Romans 8:28 in biographical form. God’s providence is not merely reactive — not the salvaging of a situation that got away from him — but his active government of all things, including hostile human choices, toward his own redemptive ends. The Roman legal machinery believed it had detained Paul. Paul knew he had been stationed (v.16, keimai). Same cell, two accounts of the world.

The same doctrine governs his response to the rival preachers, and its limits need stating precisely. Paul is not indifferent to motive — he names theirs as envy and selfish ambition, and forbids that spirit in the Philippian church in the next chapter (2:3). Nor is he indifferent to content; the man who wrote Galatians 1:8 would anathematise a preacher of another gospel. His point is narrower and sturdier: where the message is true, its power lies in the message and not in the messenger, and God is not so fastidious as to let a soul perish rather than use a flawed instrument.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul writes as a prisoner whose usefulness looked finished, to a church that was funding a mission which appeared to have stalled. He gives them no general assurance that things work out. He gives them a report: here is what God has in fact done with the wreckage — a guard evangelised, a church emboldened, and a gospel travelling on roads nobody had planned.

Now: Two applications, and they pull in different directions. For the believer whose life has been derailed — the illness that ended the work, the split that closed the ministry — verse 12 is not a demand to feel that the loss was a gain. And for the believer who is afraid to die, verses 21–23 offer not a stoic’s courage but an accountant’s logic: whether death is gain depends entirely on what you have made your life. Fill in Paul’s blank — for to me to live is — and the word that arrives unbidden will tell you what you have built on.

verseByVerse.quote: I want you to know, brothers, that what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel, so that it has become known throughout the whole imperial guard and to all the rest that my imprisonment is for Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now I want you to know, brothers and sisters, that what has happened to me has actually served to advance the gospel. As a result, it has become clear throughout the whole palace guard and to everyone else that I am in chains for Christ.

Their worry. The apostle in chains: from every angle the mission had stalled.

Advance. Prokopē, used of army pioneers cutting a road through trackless country. The chains are not a roadblock but roadworks.

The imperial guard. Praitōrion: the emperor’s elite troops. Paul was chained by the wrist to a soldier, relieved every few hours. Rome had built Paul a captive congregation and paid the guards. By the end he sends greetings from “Caesar’s household” (4:22).

For Christ. Everyone understood why he was there: not sedition, but a carpenter he said was alive. Many Christians suffer in ways that leave everyone unclear why.

Where Paul was. Probably Rome (Acts 28:16, 30), though some suggest Ephesus or Caesarea.

What it does not mean. Not a general optimism that bad things turn out fine, said too early to someone grieving. Paul reports, from inside, what God has actually done. If illness ended your work or a split closed your ministry, you are not required to feel the loss is a gain; you are invited to trust that the God who turned a prison into a pulpit is not out of options.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “imperial guard” is literally “the whole praetorium” — the Roman soldiers guarding him, or the governor’s headquarters.

verseByVerse.quote: And most of the brothers, having become confident in the Lord by my imprisonment, are much more bold to speak the word without fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And because of my chains, most of the brothers and sisters have become confident in the Lord and dare all the more to proclaim the gospel without fear.

The opposite of expected. When the leader is arrested, people usually lower their voices. Instead they grew bolder.

In the Lord. Not confident that the risk was small, but that the gospel was worth it, and that a man could pay the price and stay joyful. Contagious in a way argument is not.

Dare. Tolman. Not people who felt no fear, but who spoke anyway: the only courage there is.

A practice, not a mood. They spoke the word where it cost something.

Most. Not all. Some went quiet, and Paul says so without naming or scolding them. The New Testament never reports a revival where everyone rose to the occasion.

A textual note. Many manuscripts read “the word of God”, some “the word of the Lord”, others simply “the word”. The sense is the same.

On a Tuesday. Faithfulness under cost multiplies. If you are paying a price in obscurity, you may be doing more for those watching than you will learn in this life.

verseByVerse.quote: Some indeed preach Christ from envy and rivalry, but others from good will. The latter do it out of love, knowing that I am put here for the defense of the gospel. The former proclaim Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely but thinking to afflict me in my imprisonment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is true that some preach Christ out of envy and rivalry, but others out of goodwill. The latter do so out of love, knowing that I am put here for the defence of the gospel. The former preach Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely, supposing that they can stir up trouble for me while I am in chains.

An ugly fact. Some preached Christ in order to hurt Paul, calculating that a surge of preaching under other names would grieve a man who could no longer preach.

Selfish ambition. Eritheia, from hired political canvassing: working a crowd for yourself. It returns in 2:3, where Paul forbids it in Philippi.

Out of love. The kindest line. Paul had friends who preached because they understood what his chains were for. A wounded Christian can stop seeing the second sort.

Put here. Keimai: laid, appointed, stationed, like a sentry posted or a stone set in a foundation. Rome thinks it put him there; Paul knows he was posted.

A textual note. Later manuscripts reverse vv. 16 and 17, putting the rivals first (KJV). The earlier order puts love first.

On a Tuesday. Somewhere you did not choose (a job, a marriage, a sickbed, a town)? You are either an unlucky prisoner or a posted sentry. Same facts, not the same world.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed, and in that I rejoice. Yes, and I will rejoice,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But what does it matter? The important thing is that in every way, whether from false motives or true, Christ is preached. And because of this I rejoice. Yes, and I will continue to rejoice.

What then? A shrug: an injury set down.

What it does not mean. Not that motives do not matter; Paul calls theirs envy and forbids it (2:3). Not that any message under Christ’s name is fine; the man who wrote Galatians 1:8–9 cursed a false gospel. These rivals preached the true gospel with rotten hearts. Only that case is meant.

The power is in the message. A true gospel from a bad motive still saves. God uses flawed instruments; he has never had any other kind. The seed does not stop being seed because the sower is a scoundrel.

Why they failed. Their strategy needed Paul to care more about his standing than about Christ. Attack a man whose life is Christ by advancing Christ, and you have handed him a present.

I will rejoice. Present, then future: a decision made before he knows his verdict. Joy in this letter is chosen and commanded (3:1; 4:4).

On a Tuesday. Can you rejoice when someone you dislike does good gospel work?

verseByVerse.quote: for I know that through your prayers and the help of the Spirit of Jesus Christ this will turn out for my deliverance,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I know that through your prayers and God’s provision of the Spirit of Jesus Christ, what has happened to me will turn out for my deliverance.

A quotation. “This will turn out for my deliverance” is word for word the Greek of Job 13:16, where Job turns from his accusing friends to plead his case with God. Paul places himself in the line of the righteous sufferer vindicated through affliction.

Deliverance. Sōtēria, salvation. Not chiefly release from prison, since he does not yet know whether he will live (v. 20). Standing before God unashamed, by life or by death.

Prayers and the Spirit. Joined under one article in Greek: one supply line. The Philippians pray in Macedonia; the Spirit supplies in Rome.

Supply. Epichorēgia: the chorēgos was the wealthy citizen who funded a festival chorus’s whole cost. The Spirit does not send occasional relief; he underwrites the whole performance.

On a Tuesday. When you pray for a Christian in a hard place, you are inside the supply line. Paul could feel it arriving.

verseByVerse.quote: as it is my eager expectation and hope that I will not be at all ashamed, but that with full courage now as always Christ will be honored in my body, whether by life or by death. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I eagerly expect and hope that I will in no way be ashamed, but will have sufficient courage so that now as always Christ will be exalted in my body, whether by life or by death. For to me, to live is Christ and to die is gain.

Eager expectation. Apokaradokia: head craned forward, watching the road. Not enduring; leaning out.

Not ashamed. The fear is not execution but cracking under pressure: denying, hedging, going quiet.

In my body. In this chained, ageing body: the only place anyone honours Christ.

Life or death. Both outcomes of his trial are wins, before he knows which.

To live is Christ. Not “Christ is important” or “at the centre”, which leaves a life with Christ installed in it. Living is Christ. Take him out and nothing is left (Galatians 2:20; Colossians 3:4).

To die is gain. It follows, and only this way round. If living is Christ, death is more of him. Put anything else in the blank (family, work, health, reputation) and death is what it seems at every graveside: the end of all you had.

On a Tuesday. Fill in the blank honestly: “for to me to live is …”. The word that comes unbidden is the thing whose loss would end you.

verseByVerse.quote: If I am to live in the flesh, that means fruitful labor for me. Yet which I shall choose I cannot tell. I am hard pressed between the two. My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I am to go on living in the body, this will mean fruitful labour for me. Yet what shall I choose? I do not know. I am torn between the two: I desire to depart and be with Christ, which is better by far; but it is more necessary for you that I remain in the body.

Torn. Synechomai: squeezed from both sides. An apostle unable to choose between living and execution, because both are good.

Depart. Analysai: untying a ship, striking a tent, unyoking an ox, freeing a prisoner. Every use implies somewhere to go. Not extinction; casting off (2 Timothy 4:6).

Where the believing dead go. Immediately with Christ, consciously, and better. If death meant oblivion until the resurrection, he could not call it “far better” than fruitful work. Some, such as Seventh-day Adventists and some others, teach “soul sleep”; this verse tells against it. “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43); “away from the body and at home with the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:8).

Far better, not yet best. The best is the resurrection of the body (3:20–21). The dead are not in a corridor, but they are waiting.

Longing to die? Paul longed for Christ and left the timing to God, giving himself to those who needed him. Wanting heaven is faith; taking one’s life is not, for our times are in God’s hand (Psalm 31:15). If your longing for death has become a plan, tell someone today: a friend, a pastor, a doctor.

On your account. He wants the better thing; he chooses the useful one. Every week has that shape in miniature: the rest you have earned against the person who needs you tonight.

verseByVerse.quote: Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and continue with you all, for your progress and joy in the faith, so that in me you may have ample cause to glory in Christ Jesus, because of my coming to you again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Convinced of this, I know that I will remain, and I will continue with all of you for your progress and joy in the faith, so that through my being with you again your boasting in Christ Jesus will abound on account of me.

Convinced. Not a revelation about the trial (he still reckons with death in 2:17), but the reasoning of a man who trusts God cares about usefulness.

Progress. Prokopē again (v. 12): the gospel advancing through chains, and now the Philippians advancing. A pastor’s ambition: their movement forward and their gladness.

Joy in the faith. Gladness is not an optional temperament but something a church can grow in.

A pastoral instinct. Having said he would rather die, he does not let them feel they are the obstacle. Their growth is worth postponing heaven for.

In Christ Jesus. He imagines walking in at Philippi and the room overflowing, and directs the boasting past himself to Christ. The occasion, not the object.

Did he return? Paul was probably released and travelled again (1 Timothy 1:3), before a final imprisonment (2 Timothy 4:6).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Whatever happens, live as citizens worthy of the gospel of Christ, so that whether Paul comes or only hears, he will know they stand firm in one spirit, striving together for the faith, not frightened by opponents. This is a sign to them of destruction, and to you of salvation, from God. For it has been granted to you not only to believe in Christ but also to suffer for him, in the same struggle you saw Paul endure and now hear he still has.
verseByVerse.theology:
Suffering as a Grace-Gift

That suffering for Christ is granted — echaristhe, from charis, grace — is one of the most counter-intuitive claims in the New Testament. Not that God permits it, or merely redeems it after the fact, but that he bestows it, as he bestows faith, on those who belong to his Son. The apostles understood this when they left the Sanhedrin rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name (Acts 5:41).

Reformed theology has never treated suffering for the gospel as an aberration in the Christian life but as a feature of it in this present age: through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom (Acts 14:22). Union with a crucified and risen Lord means fellowship in both his death and his resurrection (3:10); the one cannot be taken and the other refused. A gospel that promises exemption from all hardship has misread the gift it is offering.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Philippi was a garrison colony where loyalty to the emperor was ordinary civic decency, and confessing another Lord was a visible social defection. The opposition these believers faced was not random hostility; it was the predictable friction of two citizenships in one city. Paul answers it by telling them which capital they actually belong to — a point he will make explicit at 3:20.

Now: Verse 28 forbids the bolt, not the fear; a believer who is frightened and stays put has obeyed it. And it is composure under opposition for the gospel, not opposition as such, that counts as evidence — and even that is credited to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Only let your manner of life be worthy of the gospel of Christ, so that whether I come and see you or am absent, I may hear of you that you are standing firm in one spirit, with one mind striving side by side for the faith of the gospel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever happens, conduct yourselves as citizens in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ. Then, whether I come and see you or only hear about you in my absence, I will know that you stand firm in the one Spirit, striving together as one for the faith of the gospel.

Only. Paul turns from his situation to theirs, with the command the rest of the letter unpacks.

Live as citizens. Politeuesthe, from polis. Paul had many ordinary words for “live”; he chose this one.

A colony. Philippi was a Roman colonia of retired legionaries with the ius Italicum: Roman citizens on Macedonian soil, with Roman dress, law and Latin coins, answering to a capital eight hundred miles away. Its business was to represent Rome on the frontier. So: be citizens of another capital, under another Lord. Made explicit at 3:20: “our citizenship is in heaven.”

Worthy is not moralism. A colonist does not earn citizenship by behaving well; he has it, and behaves to match.

Corporate. “Standing firm” is a battle line holding. “Striving side by side” is synathleō, competing as a team. A man alone is not a line. The answer, planted early, to 4:2.

A textual note. “In one spirit” may mean the Holy Spirit or a shared human spirit; the Greek allows both.

On a Tuesday. The test of a church is what it is like when the apostle is not in the room: on an ordinary Tuesday, with the capital far away.
verseByVerse.note: The word for “manner of life” means living as a citizen — fitting for a Roman colony proud of its status.

verseByVerse.quote: and not frightened in anything by your opponents. This is a clear sign to them of their destruction, but of your salvation, and that from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be frightened in any way by those who oppose you. This is a sign to them that they will be destroyed, but that you will be saved, and that by God.

Frightened. Ptyromenoi: used of a horse shying at a movement in the hedge. Not considered fear, but the bolt that breaks a line.

A clear sign. Endeixis, legal evidence. A small church’s steadiness reads two ways: to opponents, a hint they are on the losing side, for people do not stand like that over nothing; to the church, confirmation that they are God’s.

What it does not mean. Not that being disliked proves you right; some people are opposed because they are obnoxious. Opposition for the gospel, met without panic, is the evidence.

Not “feel no fear”. The word describes the bolt, not the pulse rate. A believer afraid who stays put has obeyed. Courage is fear refused the reins.

From God. The courage is his gift, which is why it is admissible evidence and not just bravery that week.

A textual note. Later manuscripts read “to them … but to you of salvation” (KJV) instead of “of your salvation”. The meaning is the same.

verseByVerse.quote: For it has been granted to you that for the sake of Christ you should not only believe in him but also suffer for his sake, engaged in the same conflict that you saw I had and now hear that I still have.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him, since you are going through the same struggle you saw I had, and now hear that I still have.

Granted. Echaristhē, from charis: graciously given. Two gifts under one word: believing, and suffering. Faith itself is God’s gift (Ephesians 2:8–9).

Suffering as grace. Not merely permitted or later redeemed, but bestowed, a privilege for those who belong to Christ. The apostles left the council “rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name” (Acts 5:41).

What it does not mean. Not that every hardship is persecution, or that we should seek suffering. And not prosperity teaching’s opposite error either; a gospel promising exemption from all hardship has misread the gift (Acts 14:22).

You saw. They had watched Paul stripped and beaten with rods in their marketplace and heard him sing at midnight (Acts 16:22–25).

The same conflict. Agōn, the arena: the same contest as “striving side by side” (v. 27). Paul and this church in one arena.

Fellowship. Union with Christ means sharing his sufferings and his resurrection (3:10; 1 Peter 4:13; Romans 8:17). You cannot take one and refuse the other.

For worship. If you suffer for Christ, it is neither wasted nor punishment. It is the fellowship of the cross, opening one day into the fellowship of glory.
verseByVerse.note: Paul and Silas had been beaten and jailed at Philippi.

2.title: The Mind of Christ: Humility, the Incarnation, and the Cross
2.overview:
Chapter 1 ended with a church under pressure from outside. Chapter 2 turns to the pressure inside: rivalry, conceit and grumbling, the kind of thing that later surfaces in two named women who cannot agree (4:2). Paul’s answer is not a management technique but a person. He sets before them the mind of Christ, in what may be the most important paragraph on the incarnation in the Bible (2:6–11): the one who was in the form of God did not use his equality with God for his own advantage, but emptied himself by taking the form of a slave, obeyed to the point of a slave’s death on a cross, and was therefore exalted by God to the name above every name, so that every knee will bow to him as the Lord of Isaiah 45.

Then come the consequences. Work out your salvation, because God is working in you. Stop grumbling, as Israel grumbled in the wilderness, and shine like stars in a twisted generation. Paul himself may be poured out as a drink offering, and is glad. The chapter closes with two portraits of the same mind in ordinary men: Timothy, who genuinely cares for others when everyone else looks after themselves, and Epaphroditus, the church’s courier, who nearly died bringing their gift and was more upset that they had heard he was ill than that he was.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If belonging to Christ means anything to you, if his love has comforted you, if you share the Spirit, if you have any tenderness, then make my joy complete: be of one mind, one love, one soul. Do nothing out of rivalry or vanity; in humility treat others as more important than yourselves, and look to their interests, not just your own. Think this way among yourselves, the way that is yours in Christ Jesus. He was in the form of God, yet did not treat equality with God as something to exploit. Instead he emptied himself by taking the form of a slave and being born as a man. And as a man he humbled himself further, obeying all the way to death, death on a cross. That is why God has raised him to the highest place and given him the name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee will bow, in heaven, on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Kenosis: What the Son Laid Aside, and What He Did Not

Verse 7 is the classic text for the incarnation, and its most important feature is grammatical: “he emptied himself” has no object. Paul does not say what the Son emptied himself of. He explains the emptying by what follows — “by taking the form of a servant.” The kenosis is therefore not subtraction but addition. He did not become less than God; he took to himself what he had never possessed, a full human nature.

What was laid aside was the independent exercise of divine prerogatives — the free use of what remained fully his. The glory was veiled rather than surrendered, and broke out once on the mountain to prove it had been there all along (Mark 9:2–3). This is Chalcedonian orthodoxy, which the Reformed tradition has always confessed: two natures in one person, without confusion and without division. He was not less than God in the manger, and not less than man on the cross.

Verses 10–11 raise a second question that must be answered honestly. Every knee bowing does not mean everyone is saved; the same letter speaks of opponents whose end is destruction (1:28; 3:19). Isaiah 45 itself distinguishes those who come gladly from those who come to him ashamed. Universal acknowledgement is certain; universal salvation is not taught here. The question the passage puts to the reader is not whether he will bow, but when — and in which posture.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Philippi had a status problem. Two women in the congregation could not agree (4:2), and the vocabulary Paul reaches for — eritheia, selfish ambition, the same word he used of the rival preachers in 1:17 — suggests the quarrel was less about doctrine than about position. Into that he drops the deepest thing he knows: the one with the highest claim in the universe declined to press it.

Now: The useful question in verse 6 is not “do I have a right here?” In most church conflicts you probably do. It is what you intend to do with the right you have. And verse 3 asks for a decision rather than a feeling: to count others more significant is a verb of judgement, a reckoning, not an emotion you must manufacture. Think of the person you find hardest in your congregation. Humility is not pretending you find them easy; it is deciding, before the next conversation, that what they need from it matters more than what you want from it.

verseByVerse.quote: So if there is any encouragement in Christ, any comfort from love, any participation in the Spirit, any affection and sympathy, complete my joy by being of the same mind, having the same love, being in full accord and of one mind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If being in Christ gives you any encouragement, if his love gives you any comfort, if you share in the Spirit at all, if you have any tenderness and compassion, then make my joy complete: think the same way, love the same way, be one in soul and purpose.

Four “ifs” that mean “since”. The Greek form assumes the condition is true: “if there is any encouragement in Christ, and there is …”. Paul is not doubting their experience; he is calling on it. You have been encouraged by Christ, loved, given the Spirit; now let that show in how you treat each other.

The same mind. Phroneō, Paul’s key verb in this letter (used ten times): not just an opinion but a whole way of thinking and setting the heart. Unity here is not uniformity of taste, or everyone agreeing about the church carpet. It is a shared direction: the same love, the same aim, Christ.

Why it matters so much to Paul. He is in chains, and their partnership is his joy (1:4). A church at odds with itself takes the joy out of a prisoner’s cell more surely than Nero can.

What it does not mean. Not unity at the expense of truth. The same Paul warns sharply of “dogs” in 3:2. The oneness he asks for is among people who already share the gospel; it is the end of rivalry, not the end of conviction.

On a Tuesday. Before the next difficult conversation with a fellow Christian, run through the four “ifs”. You were encouraged by Christ. You were loved when you were unlovely. You share the same Spirit with this person. Start from there.

verseByVerse.quote: Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do nothing out of rivalry or to make yourself look good. Instead, in humility, regard others as more important than yourselves. Each of you should look not only to your own interests but to the interests of others too.

Selfish ambition. Eritheia: originally the canvassing of a hired political hack, the person working an angle for himself or his faction. The same word described the rival preachers in 1:17. Conceit is kenodoxia, literally “empty glory”: wanting a reputation with nothing behind it. Notice the echo coming in verse 7: the opposite of empty glory is Christ, who emptied himself.

Humility. In the Greek world tapeinophrosynē was a slave’s quality and not a virtue at all: grovelling, servile. The gospel turned it into the crown of character, because God himself had come in the form of a slave. Christianity did not just recommend humility; it made it respectable.

What it does not mean. To “count others more significant” does not mean pretending they are more gifted than you, or despising yourself. Jesus knew he was Lord and Teacher, and washed feet (John 13:13–14). Humility is not a low opinion of yourself; it is ranking another person’s good above your own advantage. C. S. Lewis put it well: not thinking less of yourself, but thinking of yourself less.

Not only his own. Paul does not forbid looking to your own interests; “not only” assumes you will. He adds the interests of others alongside. Love your neighbour “as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18) presupposes that you do look after yourself.

On a Tuesday. In a meeting, notice who has not been heard and ask them. When a colleague gets the credit for something you did, let it go once without correcting the record. In the car park, take the far space.

verseByVerse.quote: Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have this attitude among yourselves, the very attitude that is yours because you are in Christ Jesus.

Example or union? Christians have read this verse two ways.

Most have taken it as an example: think as Christ thought. Jesus himself said, learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly (Matthew 11:29), and Peter says Christ suffered “leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps” (1 Peter 2:21).

Some scholars, notably Ernst Käsemann, argued that Paul is not offering a moral example at all. “In Christ” is the sphere of salvation, so the verse means “behave as befits those who are in Christ”, and the hymn that follows tells the story of salvation, not a model to copy.

Verdict. Both are true, and Paul holds them together. The attitude is “yours in Christ”: it belongs to you because you are united to him, and his Spirit is forming his mind in you. That is why it can be imitated at all. An example alone would only crush us; union alone, without a pattern, would leave us vague. Christ is first our Saviour and then our pattern, never the other way round.

A textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add “for” (“Let this mind be in you”, with gar). The earliest witnesses (P46, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) lack it. Probably not original; the meaning is unchanged.

For worship. What follows in verses 6–11 has the rhythm of a hymn, and many think the church already sang it before Paul quoted it. Whether he wrote it or borrowed it, Paul did his ethics by singing about Christ. Before you ask how you should treat people, look at him.
verseByVerse.note: Verses 6–11 may be an early Christian hymn.

verseByVerse.quote: who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though he existed in the very nature of God, he did not treat his equality with God as something to be used for his own advantage.

In the form of God. Morphē is not a mere outward shape. It is the form that expresses what a thing really is. The same word in verse 7, “the form of a servant”, means he was truly a slave, not one in appearance only. So here: he truly was God. “Was” is a present participle (hyparchōn): he was existing as God, continuously, before the incarnation. Compare “the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5) and “in the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1).

A thing to be grasped. Harpagmos is a rare word, and the interpretations divide.

Something to snatch, which he did not yet have (res rapienda). This would make Christ less than God, reaching for a status he lacked. It contradicts “in the form of God” and “equality”.

Something to hold on to tightly (res rapta), as if he might lose it.

Something to exploit or use for his own advantage. Roy Hoover’s study of the idiom showed that this is how the phrase works in Greek writers: treating something you already have as an asset to cash in.

Verdict. The third. He already possessed equality with God, and did not regard it as something to use for himself. That is the whole point for the Philippians: the one with every right to insist on his status did not, so you need not insist on yours.

Adam in the background. Adam, made in God’s image, reached for equality he did not have: “you will be like God” (Genesis 3:5). Christ, who had equality, let go of its privileges. The first Adam grasped and fell; the last Adam stooped and was exalted.

On a Tuesday. What do you hold as a right you can cash in: seniority, being right, years of service, your expertise? Christ had the highest right in the universe and spent it on others.

verseByVerse.quote: but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead, he emptied himself by taking the very nature of a slave, being born as a human being like us.

Emptied of what? The verb has no object. Paul never says what Christ emptied himself of. He explains the emptying by the participle that follows: “by taking the form of a servant”. The emptying is done by adding, not subtracting. He did not cease to be what he was; he became what he was not. As the old hymn says, he laid aside his glory, not his godhead. Compare “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

Kenotic theories. In the nineteenth century some theologians (Gottfried Thomasius in Germany, later Charles Gore in England) argued that the Son gave up his divine attributes, such as omniscience and omnipotence, to become man. This was an honest attempt to take his real humanity seriously, his growing in wisdom (Luke 2:52) and not knowing the day (Mark 13:32).

Why the Reformed reject it. A God who can stop being omniscient was not God to begin with; attributes are not accessories. And Scripture says that in him “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9), and that the Son “upholds the universe by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3) all through his earthly life. The church’s answer at Chalcedon (451) is better: one person, two natures, “without confusion, without change, without division, without separation”. He veiled his glory, and in his human nature he lived in dependence on the Father and the Spirit, but he never ceased to be God. The mystery is real; the kenotic solution solves it by taking away the God.

A slave. Not just a servant in the polite modern sense. Doulos: a slave, the lowest rung in Roman society, someone with no rights. Paul may have Isaiah’s Servant in mind, who “poured out his soul to death” (Isaiah 53:12), where the same idea of pouring out appears.

The likeness of men. “Likeness” does not mean he only seemed human (the Docetist error). It means he was truly like us, while being more than us, and without sin (Hebrews 4:15).

For worship. At Christmas we sing about a baby. Paul makes us see what it cost: the Lord of glory under a slave’s yoke. “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14), and he still is.

parallels.desc: he poured out his soul to death

verseByVerse.quote: And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And having appeared as a man, he humbled himself still further by obeying God all the way to death, and not just any death, but death on a cross.

Two steps down. Verse 7 is the step from God to man. Verse 8 is the step down within humanity, from man to the lowest of men. Becoming human was already humbling; he went further.

Obedient. The eternal Son, equal with the Father, “learned obedience through what he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8). Not that he was ever disobedient, but that as a man he learned in experience what obedience costs, in Gethsemane: “not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39). His obedience is not only a pattern; it is the righteousness credited to us (Romans 5:19).

Even death on a cross. Hard to feel now, with crosses on church spires and necklaces. To the Philippians, Roman citizens proud of it, it was unspeakable. Crucifixion was the slave’s punishment, the death for rebels and runaways, and Roman law generally exempted citizens from it. Cicero called it the cruellest and most disgusting penalty and said the very word should be kept far from a Roman’s eyes and ears. For a Jew it was worse still: “a hanged man is cursed by God” (Deuteronomy 21:23). So the form of a slave (v. 7) ends in the death of a slave.

What it does not mean. The cross is not merely an inspiring example of self-sacrifice. Paul uses it here as a pattern, but elsewhere he explains why it had to happen: he became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). A man drowning does not need an example of swimming; he needs to be pulled out. Christ’s humility saves before it teaches.

On a Tuesday. Most humbling on an ordinary day is small: doing the job no one notices, apologising first, staying with an elderly parent who no longer knows your name. None of it is a cross. But the cross makes such things possible and gives them dignity.
verseByVerse.note: Crucifixion was the most shameful form of Roman execution.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That is why God raised him to the highest place and gave him the name that is above every name: so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth and under the earth, and every tongue openly declare that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

Therefore. The exaltation is God’s answer to the humiliation. Jesus said it would be so: whoever humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11). He did not grab the highest place; he was given it.

The name. Which name is above every name? Not “Jesus”, which he had from birth and many others shared. The name is “Lord” (Kyrios), the word the Greek Old Testament used for God’s own name, YHWH. Verse 11 makes this clear: the confession is that Jesus Christ is Lord.

Isaiah 45. This is the decisive point for the meaning. Paul is quoting Isaiah 45:23, one of the fiercest monotheistic passages in the Bible. There the LORD says, “I am God, and there is no other”, and swears, “To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear allegiance.” Paul takes the words that belong to the one true God alone and applies them to Jesus. A first-century Jew could not say anything higher. Jesus is not a second god beside the LORD; he shares the LORD’s own name and honour, “that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father” (John 5:23). And this does not compete with the Father: it is “to the glory of God the Father”.

Will everyone be saved? Some Christians, from Origen to modern universalists, read “every knee” and “every tongue” as a promise that all will finally be saved, and link it with God reconciling “to himself all things” (Colossians 1:20).

Verdict. The text promises universal acknowledgement, not universal salvation. In Isaiah the next verse adds that all who were incensed against him shall come and be put to shame (45:24). “Under the earth” includes the dead and the defeated powers, whom Christ “disarmed” and put to open shame (Colossians 2:15). Every knee will bow: some in glad worship, others because they can no longer resist. Paul elsewhere quotes the same verse of the judgement seat (Romans 14:10–11). The question is not whether you will bow to Jesus, but whether you will do it now, gladly, or then, too late.

A textual note. “The name” has the article in the earliest manuscripts (P46, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus). Later manuscripts drop it, giving the KJV’s “a name which is above every name”. The article is almost certainly original, and it matters: not just a great name, but the name, God’s own.

For worship. The early Christian confession “Jesus is Lord” (Romans 10:9) cost people their lives when the empire demanded “Caesar is Lord”. Say it this week, and mean it, in the place you work.
verseByVerse.note: The words echo a passage where the LORD says every knee will bow to him alone; Paul applies them to Jesus.

parallels.desc: to me every knee shall bow

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–18 — Working Out What God Works In
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So, my dear friends, as you have always obeyed, not only when I was there but even more now that I am away, keep working out your salvation with reverence and trembling, because it is God who is at work in you, giving you both the will and the power to do what pleases him. Do everything without grumbling or arguing, so that you may be blameless and pure, God’s children without fault in a crooked and warped generation. Among them you shine like stars in the night sky as you hold out the word of life. Then on the day of Christ I can be proud that I did not run or work for nothing. And even if my life is poured out like a drink offering on the sacrifice of your faith, I am glad and rejoice with you all. You too should be glad and rejoice with me.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sovereignty and Responsibility in Sanctification

Verses 12–13 are the New Testament’s most exact statement of how holiness actually works, and the decisive word is the little conjunction between them. Paul does not write “work out your salvation, but remember God is working too,” as though effort and grace divided the task between them. He writes work, for God is at work. Divine agency is the ground of human effort, not its rival. The two do not compete for the same square inch; they rise and fall together.

And the working-in reaches further than the ability to obey: God works “both to will and to work.” He is beneath the desire itself. A Christian who finds in himself a genuine wish to please God is looking at evidence of grace, not of good character. This is why “fear and trembling” is the fitting posture — not the dread that God might drop him, which 1:6 has already excluded, but the seriousness of a man who has realised whose workshop he is standing in. Note also that every pronoun here is plural: Paul is telling a congregation with a quarrel in it to work this out together.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Philippians had a good record of obedience, but it had been built with an apostle available. Paul’s concern is what happens now that he is in chains and may never return — and the first sin he names is the wilderness sin of murmuring.

Now: Grumbling is the respectable Christian’s sin, and almost no one repents of it. Verse 13 is the word for the believer who feels the gap between who he is and who he longs to be: the longing itself is God’s doing.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my beloved, as you have always obeyed, so now, not only as in my presence but much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then, my dear friends, you have always obeyed, and not only when I was with you. Now that I am away, obey even more: keep working out your own salvation with reverence and trembling. For it is God who is working in you, producing both the desire and the doing, for his own good pleasure.

Work out, not work for. Katergazesthe means to bring to completion, to work something through to its end, as you might work a mine or a field. Paul is writing to people who already have salvation (1:6, 29). He is not telling them to earn it, but to live it out to the finish. Salvation here includes the whole of it: being made holy, standing firm, and reaching the final day.

Fear and trembling. Not terror that God will drop you. The phrase in Paul means reverent seriousness before God (1 Corinthians 2:3; Ephesians 6:5). You are handling holy things.

For it is God. The word “for” is the ground of the whole command. You work because God works. He works in you “to will”, the desires, and “to work”, the ability. This is the promise of the new covenant: “I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes” (Ezekiel 36:27).

How do the two fit?

Roman Catholic teaching holds that grace enables us to cooperate and so to merit an increase of justification.

Arminian Christians hold that God enables, but the final decision is ours, so the Christian can fail to work out what God began.

The Reformed view: justification is by grace alone and complete; sanctification is a real cooperation, in which we truly act, but God is the first and decisive cause even of our willing.

Verdict. Paul does not divide the work between God and us, part his and part ours. It is all God’s and all ours, at different levels: he works in, we work out. Augustine’s prayer captures it: give what you command, and command what you will. The working out is real effort, but it is sure to succeed, because the one working in is God.

What it does not mean. Some take “your own salvation” as the health of the church community, not individual salvation. Paul is speaking to the church as a body (the “you” is plural), so that is part of it; but the word sōtēria in Paul is not just community wellbeing. Each of them, together, is to press on to the end.

On a Tuesday. A gardener does not make the seed grow, but no garden flourishes without one. Get up and pray even when you do not feel like it, and then thank God that you wanted to.

verseByVerse.quote: Do all things without grumbling or disputing,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do everything without grumbling or arguing.

The wilderness echo. “Grumbling” (gongysmos) is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel muttering against God and Moses in the wilderness: about the water, the food, the leaders, the long road. “How long shall this wicked congregation grumble against me?” (Numbers 14:27). Paul will quote Moses’ farewell song in the next verse, so the comparison is deliberate. Philippi, like Israel, has been rescued and is on the way to the promised land, and the temptation is the same.

Why God takes it so seriously. It looks minor. But Moses said their grumbling was not against him but against the LORD (Exodus 16:8). Grumbling is a quiet verdict on God: he has not looked after me properly. Paul warns the Corinthians about the same thing: “nor grumble, as some of them did and were destroyed by the Destroyer” (1 Corinthians 10:10).

Disputing. Dialogismoi: arguments, quibbling, inner reasoning that turns into complaint. Not honest discussion; the kind of argument that is really about winning.

What it does not mean. Not that a Christian can never complain or lament. The Psalms are full of honest complaint brought to God. The difference is direction: lament takes the trouble to God; grumbling takes it about God to other people.

On a Tuesday. Try a day without complaining about the weather, the traffic, the boss or the church. When you notice yourself starting, turn it into a request to God or a thanks for something. Most people are surprised how often they have to stop.

verseByVerse.quote: that you may be blameless and innocent, children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and twisted generation, among whom you shine as lights in the world, holding fast to the word of life, so that in the day of Christ I may be proud that I did not run in vain or labor in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then you will be blameless and pure, children of God without fault in a crooked and warped generation. Among them you shine like stars in the world as you hold fast to the word of life. And on the day of Christ I will be able to boast that I did not run in vain or work hard for nothing.

Moses’ song turned around. “A crooked and twisted generation” is from Deuteronomy 32:5, where Moses calls Israel itself blemished, no longer God’s children because of their sin. Paul reverses it. Now the people of God are the children without blemish, and the crooked generation is the world around them. The church is the new Israel in the wilderness, and this time God means them to get it right.

Stars. Phōstēres is the word for the lights in the sky in the Greek of Genesis 1:14: “Let there be lights in the expanse of the heavens.” Daniel promises that “those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky above” (Daniel 12:3). Paul’s picture is of a dark night sky over the Roman world, and in it, small points of light: a few households in Philippi who do not grumble, cheat or lie. Jesus said the same: “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14).

Holding fast or holding out? Epechontes can mean either “holding fast to” the word or “holding it out”, offering it. Both fit. The ESV chooses “holding fast”, which suits the call to perseverance; “holding out” suits the stars shining to others. The best answer may be both: you cannot hold out what you do not hold onto.

Not in vain. Paul pictures himself as a runner and a labourer who will see on the last day whether his work in Philippi lasted. A pastor’s joy is his people’s faithfulness (1 Thessalonians 2:19–20).

On a Tuesday. Stars do not shine by trying hard; they shine because of what they are, and they show up most in the dark. A Christian nurse on a night shift who does not join the gossip about the difficult patient is shining.

parallels.desc: those who are wise shall shine

verseByVerse.quote: Even if I am to be poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrificial offering of your faith, I am glad and rejoice with you all. Likewise you also should be glad and rejoice with me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But even if my life is poured out like a drink offering on the sacrifice and service of your faith, I am glad, and I rejoice with all of you. In the same way you should be glad and rejoice with me.

The drink offering. In Israel’s worship a measure of wine was poured out over or beside a sacrifice to complete it (Numbers 15:5–10; 28:7). Pagan Philippians knew the same custom, the libation poured out to the gods at a meal or sacrifice. Paul pictures the Philippians’ faith and service as the main sacrifice, and his own life as the small offering poured out on top. He makes himself the lesser part.

Death or labour? Some take “poured out” as his ongoing toil for them. Most take it as his possible execution, which fits the trial in chapter 1 and his later words, “I am already being poured out as a drink offering” (2 Timothy 4:6). Verdict: death is in view, but the point is the same either way: his life is spent for their faith, and he counts it joy.

Glad together. Paul does not ask them to be sad for him. Joy is shared, both ways. A Christian facing death can say to friends, “Rejoice with me,” because he goes to Christ, “which is far better” (1:23).

On a Tuesday. A mother who has given her best years to raising children, or a carer worn out by a parent with dementia, may feel used up. Paul’s picture says that a life poured out on others’ faith is not wasted; it is an offering, and God receives it.
verseByVerse.note: A drink offering was wine poured out with a sacrifice, completing it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–30 — Two Men Who Show You the Mind of Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul hopes, if the Lord Jesus allows, to send Timothy to them soon, so he can be cheered by news of them. He has no one else like him, who genuinely cares about their welfare; everyone else looks after their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. They know Timothy’s proven character: like a son with his father, he has served with Paul in the gospel. Paul will send him as soon as he sees how things go for himself, and he trusts in the Lord that he will come soon too. Meanwhile he is sending back Epaphroditus, his brother, fellow worker and fellow soldier, their messenger who looked after his needs. Epaphroditus has been longing for them and was distressed that they heard he was ill. He was ill, close to death, but God had mercy on him, and on Paul too, sparing him sorrow on sorrow. So receive him with joy and honour people like him, because he nearly died for the work of Christ, risking his life to do for Paul what they could not do in person.
verseByVerse.theology:
Virtue Has to Be Seen in a Face

Reformed ethics has never treated Christian character as an abstraction. It is a way of living that exists only in particular people, and Paul’s method here follows his Lord’s: after the doctrine, a person. Timothy embodies 2:4 — looking to the interests of others — and Epaphroditus embodies 2:7–8, pouring himself out to the point of nearly dying. Neither is presented as an exceptional case. They are what the gospel ordinarily produces in people it has actually got hold of.

Two pastoral truths sit inside this section and should not be missed. First, Paul could not heal Epaphroditus. The apostle through whom God worked extraordinary miracles (Acts 19:11–12) here watched a friend nearly die and credited the recovery to mercy alone. Healing is a gift God gives as he chooses, never a technique the church operates. Second, Paul admits to sorrow, and to sorrow that could have been piled upon sorrow. The man who wrote “rejoice always” was carrying grief while he wrote it. Joy in this letter runs underneath sadness; it does not replace it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Epaphroditus had been sent from Philippi to stay and serve, and was returning early, ill and with the job unfinished. Every congregation contains people ready to draw conclusions about that. Paul heads them off before the man reaches the gate — he is not coming back a failure, he is coming back a soldier who gambled his life and lost his health doing it. The phrase “to complete what was lacking in your service to me” is not a rebuke of Philippian stinginess; what was lacking was simply the one thing some eight hundred miles prevented them from sending, their own presence.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, so that I too may be cheered by news of you. For I have no one like him, who will be genuinely concerned for your welfare.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I hope, if the Lord Jesus wills, to send Timothy to you soon, so that I too may be encouraged when I hear how you are doing. I have no one else like him, who will genuinely care about your welfare.

Why this passage is here. It can look like a travel note dropped into the middle of theology. It is not. After the hymn about Christ who looked to others’ interests, Paul shows them two living examples of the same mind. Timothy and Epaphroditus are verses 3–4 with names and faces.

In the Lord Jesus. Paul’s plans are made under the Lord (James 4:13–15). Even a letter-carrier’s schedule is held up to Christ.

No one like him. Isopsychos, literally “equal-souled”, “like-minded”. Timothy shares Paul’s own heart for them. He had been with Paul when the church at Philippi was founded (Acts 16:1–3, 12), and Paul had sent him before as his representative (1 Corinthians 4:17).

Genuinely concerned. Merimnaō is the word Paul will use in 4:6, “do not be anxious about anything”. There is a bad anxiety, which frets over our own affairs, and a right concern, which carries others’ burdens. Paul himself felt “the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches” (2 Corinthians 11:28).

On a Tuesday. Who in your church is genuinely concerned for others, without being paid to be? Thank God for them, and tell them. Churches run on such people.

verseByVerse.quote: For they all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. But you know Timothy’s proven worth, how as a son with a father he has served with me in the gospel. I hope therefore to send him just as soon as I see how it will go with me, and I trust in the Lord that shortly I myself will come also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone else looks after their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. But you know Timothy’s proven character: like a son working with his father, he has served with me in spreading the gospel. So I hope to send him as soon as I see how things go with me. And I am confident in the Lord that I myself will come soon too.

They all seek their own. A painful line. It does not mean every Christian in Rome was selfish; it means that among those Paul could have sent, none was free and willing for a long, costly trip for another church’s sake. It is the opposite of verse 4.

The interests of Jesus Christ. Looking after others is not a separate thing from serving Christ. His interests are his people. To neglect them is to neglect him (Matthew 25:40).

Proven worth. Dokimē: metal tested in the fire and found genuine. Timothy was young, apparently timid, and had a weak stomach (1 Timothy 4:12; 5:23; 2 Timothy 1:7). None of that mattered. What made him valuable was years of tested faithfulness.

As a son with a father. Not “served me” but “served with me”: Timothy is not Paul’s servant but his fellow slave of the gospel (1:1). An apprentice learning a trade at his father’s side.

On a Tuesday. If you are older, who is your Timothy? Take someone younger alongside you in some piece of service, not to lecture them but to do it together. If you are younger, look for a Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: I have thought it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus my brother and fellow worker and fellow soldier, and your messenger and minister to my need, for he has been longing for you all and has been distressed because you heard that he was ill. Indeed he was ill, near to death. But God had mercy on him, and not only on him but on me also, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meanwhile I think it necessary to send back to you Epaphroditus, my brother, fellow worker and fellow soldier, whom you sent to look after my needs. He has been longing for all of you and was distressed that you heard he was ill. And he certainly was ill; he nearly died. But God had mercy on him, and not only on him but on me as well, to spare me sorrow upon sorrow.

Who he was. Epaphroditus, a member of the church at Philippi, carried their gift to Paul in Rome (4:18) and stayed on to look after him. His name comes from Aphrodite: a man probably born into a pagan family, now a brother in Christ. Paul gives him three titles, rising from family to work to battle: brother, fellow worker, fellow soldier. And two more from the church’s side: their apostolos (messenger) and leitourgos (minister), a word with priestly overtones.

What happened. Travel from Philippi to Rome took several weeks, overland on the Via Egnatia and by sea. Somewhere along the way or in Rome he fell gravely ill. News reached Philippi, and news that they knew reached him. His distress was not for himself but that they were worried. That is the mind of Christ: looking to others’ interests even when you are the one who is sick.

Why didn’t Paul heal him? Paul had healed many (Acts 19:11–12; 28:8–9), yet here he had to wait on God’s mercy. Later he left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20) and told Timothy to take wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23).

Continuationist Christians say God still heals miraculously through gifted people today, and that Paul’s experience shows only that healing is not automatic.

Cessationists (the view of this commentary, held with respect for brothers who differ) see in these texts that even in the apostolic age the gifts of healing were signs God gave at his discretion, not a power at the apostles’ command, and that they faded as the apostolic foundation was laid.

Verdict. Both sides agree on what matters most here: Epaphroditus recovered because “God had mercy on him”. Healing is mercy, not a right, and God answers prayer for the sick (James 5:14–15), sometimes by restoring, sometimes by giving grace to bear it.

Sorrow upon sorrow. Paul does not pretend he would have been calm if his friend had died. The great apostle who said “to die is gain” would still have grieved. Christians grieve, just not “as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

On a Tuesday. When someone in hospital apologises for being a burden, they are being like Epaphroditus. Tell them what Paul implies: your care for us while you are ill is itself a gift.
verseByVerse.note: Epaphroditus had brought the Philippians’ gift to Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: I am the more eager to send him, therefore, that you may rejoice at seeing him again, and that I may be less anxious.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I am all the more eager to send him, so that when you see him again you may rejoice, and I may have less anxiety.

Less sorrow. Literally, “that I may be less sorrowful”. Paul is still in chains, still facing trial. Sending away his helper will cost him. But their joy at seeing Epaphroditus will lighten his own load. Love is willing to lose a comfort so that others gain one.

Possibly a defence. Some suspect Paul is also protecting Epaphroditus from criticism, in case anyone in Philippi thought he had come home early and failed in his mission. Paul makes clear he is sending him: it was Paul’s decision, not desertion.

On a Tuesday. Sometimes the kindest thing a leader can do is release a worker who needs to go home, and make sure everyone knows they leave with honour.

verseByVerse.quote: So receive him in the Lord with all joy, and honor such men, for he nearly died for the work of Christ, risking his life to complete what was lacking in your service to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So welcome him in the Lord with great joy, and honour people like him, because he came close to death for the work of Christ. He risked his life to complete the service to me that you could not give in person.

Honour such men. Paul does not say “honour the apostles” but “honour people like this”: ordinary believers who risk themselves in service. The church is to honour faithfulness, not just prominence (1 Corinthians 16:18; 1 Thessalonians 5:12–13).

Risking his life. Paraboleusamenos: a gambler’s word, staking everything on a throw. In the early church a group of Christians who nursed the sick during plagues, when everyone else fled, took the name parabolani, “the reckless ones”, from this word. During a plague in Carthage around 252, Bishop Cyprian urged Christians to care for the sick and dying, pagans included, and many did so at the cost of their lives.

What was lacking. Not a criticism of the Philippians. They could not all go to Rome. Epaphroditus did in person what the church wanted to do but could not; he made their love present.

A textual note. Manuscripts differ: “the work of Christ” (Vaticanus and others), “the work of the Lord” (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus), or simply “the work” (Ephraemi). “Of Christ” is probably original, and in any case the meaning is the same: the work was Christ’s.

For worship. The chapter that began with the Son of God taking the form of a slave and going to death ends with a man from a pagan family nearly dying to carry a gift to a prisoner. The pattern has been reproduced. That is what the gospel does. Thank God for the Epaphrodituses who have looked after you.
